newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - US Mega-malls spur Japan retail Big Bang.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - US Mega-malls spur Japan retail Big Bang.

text.p: American mega-mall developers, lured by visions of well-heeled consumers with a yen for one-stop shopping, see potential profits in a market once dominated by tiny family-run stores.

Experts agree Japan is in the throes of a retail revolution which promises more and bigger shopping centres likely to lure growing numbers of foreign retailers. But they say pitfalls await non-Japanese developers operating on their own.

"For American developers, the question is whether they can pass through the regulatory barriers," said Byron Gill, an analyst at Salomon Brothers Asia. "My guess is that they can do it, but that it could take a lot longer than they thought."

Japan's retail landscape, once dominated by a myriad of small shops clustered in shopping streets near train stations, has undergone huge changes following the 1992 relaxation of the Large-scale Retail Store Law -- for decades a barrier to the opening of big stores and still a target of foreign complaints.

"Everyone is talking about a 'Big Bang' in finance, but a 'Big Bang' has already started in retail due to deregulation of the Large-scale Retail Store Law and the fall in land prices due to the bursting of the (asset price) bubble," said Takayuki Suzuki, retail analyst at Merrill Lynch Japan.

"In the areas outside Tokyo there are lots of 'ghost towns' where there used to be shopping streets around the train stations because suburban shopping centres are taking away business," Suzuki said. "All that's left around the stations are some pachinko (pinball) parlours and a few eateries."
The United States has more than 41,000 shopping centres. Japan, just under 2,500.
But the trend toward more and bigger shopping centres is expected to persist, given more space to develop as factories move overseas and a growing demand for one-stop shopping.
U.S. retailers like GAP Inc and Spiegel Inc's Eddie Bauer unit, meanwhile, are coming to Japan in growing numbers to meet consumer demand which domestic firms can't handle.
"Japan's retail market is being 'occupied' by foreign retailers because Japan doesn't have its own stores to satisfy customers," said Suzuki.
AMERICAN DEVELOPERS EYE AFFLUENT JAPAN SHOPPERS

Japanese mall development to date, however, has been dominated by domestic retailers, such as supermarket chains JUSCO Co Ltd, Daiei Inc, and MYCAL Corp, which analysts say lack the management expertise honed by Americans over decades.
Now U.S. developers are hoping get into the Japanese act, a move likely to spur further entry by U.S. retailers into the market, but clearly not a prospect everyone here welcomes.

"Smaller shopping centres...saw the arrival of big operators like JUSCO as a kind of 'Black Ships,'" said Susumu Inamura, a spokesman for the Japan Council of Shopping Centres, alluding to the U.S. Naval ships under Commodore Matthew Perry whose arrival in 1854 pushed Japan to open to the West.
"Now the real 'Black Ships' are coming with the arrival of the foreigners," Inamura said.

American Malls International Japan Ltd (AMI Japan), for one, argues its development and mall-management experience can help fill a "huge hunger" among Japanese consumers for a wide selection of goods and entertainment at better prices.
Set up last year by veteran mall developer Herbert Miller, AMI plans to build about eight 250,000 square metre "mega-malls" near big population centres, AMI Japan Vice President John Diefenbach.
"Our business is to bring together the best possible mix of retail and entertainment merchants and to create an exciting environment to help them succeed," Diefenbach told Reuters.
"By contrast, the Japanese mall owner is usually a retailer himself and his selection of stores is limited by the need to promote his own product lines," he added.
HURDLES HIGH FOR FOREIGN DEVELOPERS
AMI's ambitious plans, however, have run into some snags.

The U.S. developer's plan to build the first of its one-kilometre long "Retail Theme Parks" in the town of Moriya, 35 km (20 miles) northeast of Tokyo, is opposed by Agriculture Ministry officials who do not want existing farmland to be re-zoned for commercial purposes. Industry sources also say some trade ministry officials are against the plan because of outcries from smaller local retailers.

Diefenbach said AMI believes it can get approval for the project in what he termed one of the fastest-growing residential areas in eastern Japan, but industry experts said delays could ultimately undermine its profitability.

"The legal situation is unique, so they can't just jump in," said Susumu Inamura, a spokesman for the Japan Council of Shopping Centres. "The Large-scale Retail Store Law has been liberalised, but there are lots of other laws administered by lots of other ministries. It could take five or six years for the project to get up and running."

Such pitfalls are one reason AMI rival WPI.Koll Pacific Advisors, a joint venture between affiliates of real estate firms World Premier Investments (WPI) and Koll Asia Pacific, is taking a different approach.

"Deregulation is proceeding in Japan, but one can't say it's really open. It's still a closed society and a closed economic environment," said Fumie Kadokura, executive director of MGS Japan Co Ltd, a Japanese consortium which last year retained WPI.Koll as a consultant to would-be Japanese mall developers.

MGS and WPI.Koll have identified five potental mall sites for development by Japanese consortia, Kadokura said, adding WPI.Koll was still pondering whether Japanese shopping mall projects would be attractive targets for direct investment.

U.S. real estate developer Trammell Crow, meanwhile, last year teamed up with a Japanese partner in MC-Trammell Crow Retail Ltd to consult on retail concepts and advise American companies looking for mall and other retail locations in Japan.
"Trammell Crow has lots of retail tenants in the United States and lots of them want to come to Japan," said MC-Trammell Crow Retail Director Yoshitaka Miyamura.
While U.S. developers test the waters, domestic property and railway companies are also catching shopping mall mania.

Railway company Tokyu Corp, for example, is considering developing an American-style shopping mall in Minami-Machida between Yokohama and Tokyo and is interested in attracting U.S. retailers as potential tenants, a company spokesman said.
U.S. developers, however, hope to have an edge when it comes to attracting foreign tenants, a factor analysts agree is critical to shopping mall success.

"American (retail) companies are happy to take the risk (of coming to Japan), but they want a risk that they can understand and American mall developers here would facilitate that process," said a U.S. embassy official.
